        The death toll from a Russian strike on an ammunition depot in Ukraine's Kyiv region has risen to 38, with four people still missing, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday.
The deadliest Russian strike in the Kyiv area this year took place late Friday as Moscow launched an intense campaign of attacks on the Ukrainian capital, which has continued over the weekend.
Friday's blast hit a military facility that held artillery shells, mines, drones and other ammunition.
Zelenskyy said on Telegram that first responders had managed to extinguish most of the fires. However, the scale of contamination in the area was significant and this work would continue for as long as necessary.
The president released video footage showing firefighting teams battling blazes and removing debris from destroyed buildings.
In its intensified attacks on the country, Russia over the last week launched nearly 2,000 strike drones, more than 1,600 aerial bombs, and 31 missiles, including North Korean ballistic missiles, Zelenskyy said.
"We are seeking just responses to every Russian strike and crime. They will certainly come," he said.
Overnight Saturday, plumes of black smoke poured over the capital's western suburbs, while videos published by Ukraine's rescue services showed homes near the blast epicenter in flames, reported Agence France-Presse (AFP).
The attack was the second to hit a munitions depot near Kyiv in less than two months, with officials expressing anger that arms were still being stored so close to residential areas.
Both Russia and Ukraine have intensified long-range strikes on each other in recent months, pushing civilian casualties to their highest level since Moscow invaded in 2022.
"Those who allowed this to happen must be held accountable for their decisions ... ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential areas," President Zelenskyy said in a post on X.
The blast forced hundreds to evacuate and damaged multiple homes, including a care facility for elderly and disabled people, he added.
The mayor of the nearby town of Dmytrivka were also among the dead, Kyiv region Gov. Tymur Tkachenko said on Telegram.
Residents in the area told AFP the explosion was "terrifying."
"We thought we were being bombed. No one knew it was a detonation," said Yana Done

corpus.title: At least 37 killed after Russian strike hits an ammunition depot near Kyiv, triggering massive explosions. Many of the victims were residents of a nearby care home.
corpus.signal_text:
At least 37 killed after Russian strike hits an ammunition depot near Kyiv, triggering massive explosions. Many of the victims were residents of a nearby care home.
The Russian army struck the village of Myla on the outskirts of Kyiv on the evening of August 28, setting fire to a warehouse where ammunition was being stored. The fire triggered a series of detonations, sending flames into nearby private homes. The explosions were powerful enough that authorities shut down traffic entirely on the Zhytomyr highway between the 15th and 32nd kilometer markers. Nearly 400 people were evacuated from the area affected by the strike.
Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Regional Military Administration, said Saturday morning that at least 27 people had been killed in the Russian strike on Myla, in Kyiv region’s Bucha district. Another 42 people, including four children, were injured to varying degrees. Among the dead was Taras Didych, head of the Dmytrivka community in the Kyiv region, who had been helping rescue people from the fire.
Update. As of 2:00 p.m. Saturday, 37 people are known to have died in the Russian strike, Tymur Tkachenko wrote.
About 50 residential buildings were damaged. The heaviest damage was to a nearby care home for elderly and disabled residents, where 20 people died, according to local social media pages.
Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the care home had been damaged. “Those who allowed this must certainly bear responsibility for their decisions. Investigators from the National Police and the Security Service of Ukraine are conducting a pretrial investigation, and a criminal case has been opened over official negligence. There are rules: ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential buildings. There will definitely be appropriate conclusions,” the president of Ukraine said.
Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi called what happened in the Bucha district the result of “criminal negligence,” recalling the “terrible tragedy in Vyshneve,” which he said “did not serve as a lesson.” Russian forces struck a Ukroboronprom warehouse in Vyshneve, near Kyiv, in July. The resulting detonation damaged 300 residential buildings and killed nine people.
The Kyiv region declared August 30 a day of mourning for those killed in the Russian strike.

"A terrible situation and terrible negligence on the part of those who stored explosives right next to people," Zelenskyy said late on August 29 in his nightly video address.
The death count now stands at 38.
Zelenskyy said the Russian drone strike was on an ammunition storage site "that definitely shouldn’t have been there.... Shells, mines, other ammunition, and drones detonated."
He added that a criminal investigation was under way.
"All the facts must be fully investigated. Another such crime -- after what happened in Vyshneve -- is absolutely unacceptable. I expect the details to be presented to the public promptly," he said.

corpus.title: Death Toll From Russian Strike On Kyiv Region Rises To 38
corpus.signal_text:
KYIV -- The death toll from an overnight Russian drone strike on Ukraine’s Bucha district in the Kyiv region has risen to 38, as rescue operations continued on August 29 and officials fear that the toll could rise further.
Tymur Tkachenko, a top district administration official, said on his Telegram channel that rescuers and relevant services continued to work at the scene.
Local authorities say the August 28 drone strike in the Kyiv region caused a major fire and explosions at a nearby warehouse, which is said to be the major cause of the casualties.
Tkachenko said that dozens of people including children, suffered injuries in the attack, which caused a large fire that spread to residential buildings in the village of Myla.
Earlier, he had said that the death toll may not be final and expressed his "sincere condolences to the families and loved ones” of those affected.
Reporting from the scene, RFE/RL’s Ukrainian Service correspondent Maryan Kushnir said that “the whole area is in ruins,” adding that the strike also affected a nursing home, where “many” people were killed.
According to Tkachenko, those killed in Bucha also included the head of the Dmytrivka community in the district, Taras Didych. The district official said it was a “great loss” for the region.
Tkachenko said an operational headquarters has been set up in Dmytrivka to provide food as well as other support to the people in the affected region.
Fireballs In The Sky
Multiple media outlets and video footage circulating on social media show an explosion followed by fireballs rising into the sky.
Ukraine's Prosecutor-General's Office said in a statement that an investigation had been launched to look into the apparent placement and storage of explosives near residential areas.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said more than 300 emergency service employees are working on the rescue operations.
"There was a strike on the warehouse followed by a detonation. Unfortunately, there is significant destruction of the surrounding infrastructure -- residential buildings, a boarding house for the elderly and people with disabilities were damaged," Zelenskyy said.
As sounds of detonations continued in the village, local resident Zhanna told RFE/RL that she had lost her husband in the incident, adding that he had previously survived the Russian occupation.

Source: Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko
